lead: Send pulses fast enough and each one is still ringing when the next one is sampled. The tails of the other symbols land on the sampling instant as intersymbol interference (ISI) and push the sample towards the wrong decision. Nyquist's first criterion states exactly when the spill is zero: the overall pulse must pass through zero at every sampling instant except its own. It also sets the floor on bandwidth, half the symbol rate. Every baseband modem and DSL line is designed around it.
prereq: You need: the Fourier transform and power spectral density (see Foundations: signals, noise and random processes), and PAM and line codes (see Sampling and pulse modulation).

sections.h3: The model: one pulse per symbol

blocks.text: A baseband link sends one symbol every T seconds. T is the symbol period. The k-th symbol ak is one of M real levels: ±1 for binary, ±1 and ±3 for 4-level PAM. The symbol rate is Rs = 1/T baud, where one baud is one symbol per second. Each symbol carries log₂M bits, so the bit rate is Rb = Rs log₂M bit/s.

The transmit filter gT(t), the channel c(t) and the receive filter gR(t) shape the pulse. Their cascade is one overall pulse p(t) = gT(t) * c(t) * gR(t), where * is convolution. Take p(0) as the peak height of one symbol at the sampler.
Here r(t) is the waveform reaching the sampler, the sum runs over every symbol n, and n(t) is the noise.
Sample at t = kT to decide symbol k. Split the sum into the term n = k and all the others:
y(kT) = ak p(0) + Σn≠k an p((k − n)T) + n(kT)
Here the first term is the wanted one, the middle sum is the ISI, and n(kT) is the noise sample.

The ISI depends on the samples p(±T), p(±2T), … of the overall pulse. The worst case comes when every neighbour has the sign that hurts. Its size, as a fraction of the wanted height, is the peak distortion D = Σn≠0 |p(nT)| / p(0). D ≥ 1 means some data patterns are decided wrongly even with no noise.
Make every ISI term zero: require p(0) ≠ 0 and p(nT) = 0 for every integer n ≠ 0. This is Nyquist's first criterion, the zero-ISI condition. Between the instants the pulse is free.
In frequency the same condition reads: the spectrum P(f), copied at every multiple of 1/T and added, must be flat.
Σm P(f − m/T) = T·p(0) for all f
Here P(f) is the Fourier transform of p(t) and the sum runs over all integers m.

The narrowest spectrum that can be flat after this folding is a rectangle of height T from −1/(2T) to +1/(2T). Its pulse is the sinc: p(t) = sin(πt/T)/(πt/T), which is 1 at t = 0 and zero at every t = nT, n ≠ 0. So zero ISI needs at least
Here BN is the Nyquist bandwidth: half the symbol rate. Any narrower spectrum leaves gaps after folding and cannot meet the criterion.
For binary, R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>, so the best is 2 bit/s per hertz; with M levels it becomes 2 log₂M bit/s/Hz. Figure 5.1.1 shows the worked example's three pulses and the sample they build.

sections.h3: Why the sinc is not the answer

blocks.text: The sinc meets the criterion in the narrowest band, but it fails in practice for two reasons. It runs from −∞ to +∞, so it is non-causal and can only be approximated with a long delay. Its tails fall only as 1/t, so a small timing error leaves many neighbours far from their zeros, and their contributions add up. The second worked example puts numbers on this.

A pulse can meet the criterion in other ways. An NRZ rectangle of width T is zero at every other sampling instant, so it has no ISI on paper; but its spectrum T·sinc(fT) never ends, and a band-limited channel rounds and spreads it. The practical answer is a pulse with a little more bandwidth than BN and fast-dying tails: the raised cosine of pulse shaping and the eye pattern.

items: The criterion is on the overall pulse p(t). A clean transmit filter followed by a distorting channel still gives ISI; that is the job of the equalizer.
It removes ISI only. Noise, crosstalk and interference remain.
It holds at the ideal sampling instants. A clock that samples early or late moves every neighbour off its zero.

examples.question: A binary baseband link sends 2400 bit/s. The overall pulse has p(0) = 1 and p(±T) = 0.25, and all other samples p(nT) are zero. Around the k-th symbol the levels are a<sub>k−1</sub> = +1, a<sub>k</sub> = −1, a<sub>k+1</sub> = +1. Find the symbol rate, the symbol period and the Nyquist bandwidth. Then find the ISI and the sample y(kT) with no noise, the peak distortion, and the margin left to the decision threshold at 0.
steps: Binary: log₂2 = 1 bit per symbol, so R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub> = 2400 baud.
y(kT) = a<sub>k</sub>p(0) + ISI = (−1)(1) + 0.5 = −0.5. The sample is still negative, so the decision −1 is right.
Without ISI the sample would be −1, at distance 1 from the threshold. Now it is −0.5, at distance 0.5: this data pattern, the worst case, has eaten half the noise margin, exactly D = 0.5.
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 2400 baud, T = 416.7 µs, B<sub>N</sub> = 1200 Hz; ISI = +0.5, y(kT) = −0.5, D = 0.5, margin halved from 1 to 0.5.

examples.question: A link uses the ideal sinc pulse, but its sampler fires 0.1T late. Take the three nearest neighbours on each side (n = ±1, ±2, ±3) and find the wanted sample p(0.1T), each neighbour's contribution p((n + 0.1)T), and the worst-case peak distortion.
steps: D = 0.3630/0.9836 = 0.369. With the worst data pattern the sample of a +1 symbol falls to 0.9836 − 0.3630 = 0.621.
More neighbours make it worse: the magnitudes fall only as 1/n, so the sum keeps growing.
examples.answer: A 10 % timing error turns zero ISI into D = 0.369 from six neighbours alone, and the worst sample drops from 1 to 0.62. This is why the sinc is not used.

traps: Using R<sub>s</sub> where R<sub>s</sub>/2 belongs. The minimum bandwidth is half the symbol rate: 2400 baud needs 1200 Hz, not 2400 Hz.
Mixing bit rate and symbol rate. B<sub>N</sub> = R<sub>s</sub>/2 uses the symbol rate; for 4-PAM at 4800 bit/s, R<sub>s</sub> = 2400 baud and B<sub>N</sub> = 1200 Hz.
Dropping the signs in the ISI sum. ISI adds with the sign of each neighbour; only the peak distortion uses magnitudes.
Writing the criterion as p(t) = 0 for t ≠ 0. It is only at the instants t = nT; between them the pulse is free.

quiz.q: State Nyquist's first criterion for zero ISI in the time domain.
quiz.a: p(0) ≠ 0 and p(nT) = 0 for every integer n ≠ 0, where p(t) is the overall pulse from transmit filter through channel to receive filter and T is the symbol period.

quiz.q: Why does the sinc pulse give zero ISI?
quiz.a: p(t) = sin(πt/T)/(πt/T) has a zero numerator whenever t/T is a nonzero integer, so a symbol's pulse is exactly zero at every other symbol's sampling instant.

quiz.q: A 4-level PAM system runs at 4800 baud with Nyquist pulses of the least bandwidth. Find the bandwidth, the bit rate and the bandwidth efficiency.
quiz.a: B<sub>N</sub> = 4800/2 = 2400 Hz. R<sub>b</sub> = 4800 × log₂4 = 9600 bit/s. Efficiency = 9600/2400 = 4 bit/s/Hz, which is 2 log₂4.

quiz.q: The overall pulse has p(0) = 2 and p(±T) = 0.3, all other samples zero. The symbols are a<sub>k−1</sub> = a<sub>k</sub> = a<sub>k+1</sub> = +1. Find the ISI, the sample and the peak distortion.
quiz.a: ISI = 0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6. y(kT) = (1)(2) + 0.6 = 2.6. D = (0.3 + 0.3)/2 = 0.3. These neighbours help; the pattern −1, +1, −1 would give 2 − 0.6 = 1.4.

quiz.q: An NRZ rectangle of width T is zero at every other sampling instant. Explain why it still causes ISI in a real link.
quiz.a: At the ideal instants it meets the criterion. But its spectrum T·sinc(fT) has no upper limit. A channel of finite bandwidth removes the high frequencies, so the received pulse is rounded and lasts longer than T; its tails then reach the neighbouring sampling instants as ISI.

quiz.q: Using the second worked example, explain why the ISI from a timing error grows with the length of the sinc, while a fast-decaying pulse does not show this.
quiz.a: With a 0.1T error each neighbour contributes about 0.1/n in size, so the sum behaves like the harmonic series and keeps growing (0.363 from six neighbours). A pulse whose tails fall as 1/n³ gives a sum that settles after a few terms, so the ISI stays small.

beyond: Faster-than-Nyquist signalling sends symbols closer than T on purpose and removes the known ISI with a sequence detector instead of a filter. Partial-response signalling, met later in this unit, also accepts a known ISI. Search for Nyquist ISI criterion, faster-than-Nyquist signalling and peak distortion to go further.

figure.caption: The worked example's three symbols, +1, −1, +1, each with p(0) = 1 and p(±T) = 0.25 (dashed), and their sum (solid). At t = kT the two neighbours add +0.25 each, so the sample is −0.5 instead of −1: half the margin to the threshold is gone.

spec.aria: Plot of three pulses centred at minus one, zero and plus one symbol periods, with heights plus one, minus one and plus one, and their sum. At time zero the sum is minus 0.5, made of minus 1 from the own pulse and plus 0.25 from each neighbour.
